synthesis.executiveSummary:
Four days out, the athlete is fresher than he thinks and slower than Garmin thinks. The block did not collapse — CTL fell 24% from its 2026-08-02 peak (72.3 → 54.8), not the 63% Garmin's own chronic-load figure implies, because Garmin's chronic is a ~15-31 day estimator, not a 42-day EWMA. VO2max never moved (53.0; maxMet actually rose 0.28% across the layoff, 15.0785 → 15.1201). Training status is MAINTAINING, never DETRAINING. What IS real: a 10-day zero-running gap 2026-08-23 to 09-01, and only 19.97 km of genuine running in the 17 days to today. But he ran 7.65 km at 4:44.6/km yesterday (2026-09-07, avg HR 159) — a session that exists only in the raw FIT corpus and is absent from summarizedActivities.json, so every summary-driven view of this athlete is one run stale.

AS OF 2026-09-08: CTL 54.8, ATL 39.2, TSB +15.6. Projected race day 2026-09-12: CTL 49.9, ATL 22.2, TSB +27.7 — deeply tapered, arguably over-tapered.

THE RACE PLAN IS TOO FAST. 4:45/km is 17 s/km quicker than his best-ever CONTINUOUS 21 km (2026-07-19: 21.14 km at 5:02.4/km, avg HR 174, 0.6 min stopped) — run at CTL ~70 which he no longer has. The 4:35/km move is 27 s/km quicker than that and 8 minutes faster than his stopped-clock PR. Garmin's 1:38:25 is real but Garmin over-predicts this athlete by 8.8-13.0% against three realised efforts, including a 26:49 marathon miss on the very morning he ran it. Target 4:55/km (1:43:48), fallback 5:05/km (1:47:14).

THE 100 KM PEAK IS NOT SUPPORTABLE and is not close. Best week ever 57.12 km; last four complete weeks average 19.2 km/wk; Garmin's own running-tolerance ceiling is 40,627 impact units ≈ 34 km/week and would need to grow 2.7× faster than it ever has to reach 100 km. The number the data supports is a 50 km peak in week 3, off a 35 km opener.

correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: Training fell apart over the last month; the athlete is detrained and starts the marathon build from zero.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: A dip, not a collapse. CTL (42-day EWMA on activityTrainingLoad) fell from its peak of 72.3 on 2026-08-02 to 54.8 today — 24%. Garmin's own dailyTrainingLoadChronic fell 684 (2026-07-19) → 253 (2026-09-07), 63%, but that field decays on a ~15-31 day constant and exaggerates. VO2max is unchanged at 53.0: MetricsMaxMetData maxMet 15.0785 on 2026-08-22 → 15.1201 on 2026-09-02, UP 0.28% across the layoff. TrainingHistory reads MAINTAINING / NO_CHANGE, and was RECOVERY, never DETRAINING. Weekly volume for the four complete weeks to 2026-08-31: 27.16 / 34.77 / 0.00 / 14.83 km. Genuine running in the 17 days to today: 4.835 (Sóller 09-02) + 7.489 (treadmill 09-05, real) + 7.650 (09-07) = 19.97 km.
correctedFacts.soWhat: Aerobic capacity is intact; only recent-load accumulation is down. That is a 2-3 week problem, not a season problem — and the fitness lost is the kind that returns fast. The freshness gained is real and should be spent on Saturday, not hoarded.

correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: Garmin's 1:38 prediction is the best current estimate of race capability.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: Exactly right, and exactly stale-optimistic. RunRacePredictions, calendarDate 2026-09-07 (timestamp 2026-09-06T23:03:42Z): raceTimeHalf 5905 s = 1:38:25 (4:39.9/km); raceTimeMarathon 12972 s = 3:36:12. But it is 4:49 slower than his own best-ever prediction of 1:33:36 (2026-05-07), and Garmin over-predicts THIS athlete consistently. Three same-day calibration points: marathon predicted 3:26:16 on 2026-05-10, actual 3:53:05 → 1.130; half predicted 1:35:17 on 2026-07-19, actual 21.14 km continuous in 1:46:33 at HR 174 → 1.118; half predicted 1:36:15 on 2026-07-26, actual 1:44:44 timer → 1.088. Median 1.118, which applied to 5905 s gives 1:50:01.
correctedFacts.soWhat: Do not race off 1:38:25 — treat it as the ceiling of the possible, not the target. rocket should store a per-athlete Garmin calibration multiplier (currently 1.118) and surface predicted × multiplier, never the raw prediction.

correctedFacts.topic: "Resting heart rate is stored as 86 against a true 45"
correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: Garmin holds a wrong RHR of 86 that is corrupting the heart-rate zones; the real resting rate is 45.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: Both numbers exist; neither means what was assumed. 86 sits in 144449296_heartRateZones.json as restingHeartRateUsed, with restingHrAutoUpdateUsed = false and no timestamp — frozen at onboarding, and never measured anywhere (143 non-null UDSFile restingHeartRate days span 54-87 and 86 never appears). BUT it is arithmetically inert: trainingMethod is HR_MAX and the floors 100/118/137/157/176 are exactly 51/60/70/80/90% of maxHeartRateUsed 196 (0.60×196=117.6→118, 0.70×196=137.2→137, 0.80×196=156.8→157, 0.90×196=176.4→176). Karvonen with RHR 86 would put zone 1 at 141, not 100. Meanwhile 45 is not his resting HR either — it is his daily MINIMUM (UDSFile minHeartRate = 45 on 2026-09-07). Garmin's measured smoothed RHR today is 57, raw daily 50. The series is dense and trending well: 84 (2026-03-28) → 57 (2026-09-07), n=143, median 60, min 54.
correctedFacts.soWhat: The 86 corrupts nothing on the watch today, but it is a landmine for anything downstream applying heart-rate reserve — rocket included. Never ingest restingHeartRateUsed; ingest the UDSFile daily series. And label 45 as "overnight minimum", not resting HR, or the athlete keeps mis-comparing two different quantities.

correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: Garmin recently detected a new max heart rate of 195.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: 195 appears nowhere in the export — not as maxHeartRateUsed (196), not as any activity maxHr, not as any UDS daily maximum. Actual recorded maxima: 201 (2026-06-14, a 9.86 km run at 4:58/km, avg HR 175), 199 (2026-04-11), 196 (2026-04-25), then three at 194. The only activity carrying time above 196 is that 2026-06-14 run: 12 s in hrTimeInZone_6.
correctedFacts.soWhat: Zones are built 5 bpm low, so every ceiling above zone 1 is 3-5 bpm too tight (rebuilt on 201 the floors would be 100/121/141/161/181). This does not affect the raw "HR under 170" trigger, but it invalidates any %-of-max translation: 170 is 86.7% of the profile max and 84.6% of his real one.

correctedFacts.topic: UNASKED — summarizedActivities.json is one run stale
correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: The summary JSON is the complete activity record; 2026-09-05 was the last session.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: UploadedFiles_0-_Part1.zip holds 57 activity FIT files against 56 activities in the JSON. The orphan is luisdeburnaybastos@gmail.com_479581793159.fit: start_time 2026-09-07T19:09:02Z, sport running, total_distance 7649.85 m, total_timer_time 2175.711 s (36:16 = 4:44.6/km), total_elapsed 2241.706 s, avg_heart_rate 159, max_heart_rate 175, total_ascent 54 m, 8 laps, 2182 records at 1 Hz. Filenames are 12-digit UPLOAD ids with zero overlap with 11-digit activityIds — join on file_id.time_created vs startTimeGmt/1000 (tolerance 2 s; max observed offset across the 56 matches is 1.0 s).
correctedFacts.soWhat: Any ingest keyed off the summary JSON silently drops yesterday's session. Including it moves today's numbers from CTL 52.3 / ATL 26.5 / TSB +25.8 to CTL 54.8 / ATL 39.2 / TSB +15.6 — a 10-point TSB swing on the single most decision-relevant metric, four days before a race.

correctedFacts.topic: UNASKED — the 2026-09-05 "10 km treadmill" is really 7.49 km
correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: The last hard session was a 10.00 km treadmill run at 4:55/km.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: activityId 24251846565. Top-level distance is exactly 1000000.0 cm (a suspiciously round 10.000 km), but splitSummaries[type=3] — the whole-session split, its duration 2953.51 s matching the top-level duration exactly — says 7488.69 m at averageSpeed 2.536 m/s. The raw FIT agrees: last cumulative record.distance 7488.68 m, and integrating enhanced_speed over 2954 1 Hz records gives 7488.72 m. Third check: steps 7316 × avgStrideLength 102.62 cm = 7508 m. avgSpeed was rescaled to match the override (0.3386 × 10 × 2953.5 = 10000 m); stride, steps and splits were not. Control case 2026-08-15 is self-consistent at 5752.88 m both ways. True pace 6:34/km, not 4:55/km. The error has already propagated into Garmin's own data: RunningTolerance acuteDistance jumped 4834 → 14834 m on 2026-09-05, exactly +10000.
correctedFacts.soWhat: The most recent "hard" session is 2.5 km shorter and 1:39/km slower than recorded. It inflates the trailing-30-day window, the pace history, and Garmin's own tolerance figure. rocket must quarantine it — and this is precisely the corruption class that only a summary-vs-records reconciliation catches.

correctedFacts.topic: UNASKED — the 1:44:44 half PR is not a race
correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: The half-marathon PR of 1:44:44 is the benchmark to beat.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: personalRecord.json Best Half Marathon = 6284.099 s on activityId 23744064058 (2026-07-26), and that value equals the activity's `duration` (timer time) exactly. But elapsedDuration is 7245.70 s — 961.6 s (16:02) of stopped time, across 22 laps, at avg HR 165 with 85.9 min in zone 4. Garmin also awarded it on a track measured at 21,096.49 m, 1.01 m SHORT of 21,097.5 m. His best CONTINUOUS 21 km is 2026-07-19: 21.14 km at 5:02.4/km (1:46:33), avg HR 174, max 194, only 0.6 min stopped, aerobicTrainingEffect 5.0, label VO2MAX, load 431.5 — the single hardest session in the record.
correctedFacts.soWhat: The right benchmark for Saturday is 1:46:33 continuous at HR 174, not 1:44:44 with the clock stopped. That reframes the whole target: 4:55/km (1:43:48) is a decisive genuine improvement, whereas 4:45/km demands a 17 s/km jump on 29% less chronic fitness.

correctedFacts.topic: UNASKED — there is no sleep or HRV data at all
correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: Sleep and HRV are sparse but usable as recovery inputs.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: Two overnight sleep sessions exist in the entire export (2026-06-25, 2026-07-18) out of 161 sleepData entries; 155 are the bare placeholder {"retro": false}. The most recent night is 52 days ago. HRV exists as exactly two scalars (59.0 and 67.0 ms) in healthStatusData, both status ONBOARDING with baselineUpperLimit = baselineLowerLimit = 0.0. TrainingReadinessDTO.hrvWeeklyAverage is frozen at 511.0 on all 267 records, and hrvFactorPercent / stressHistoryFactorPercent are 0 with feedback NONE on 267/267 — Garmin's own readiness engine has never once consumed HRV or stress for this athlete. Readiness on 2026-09-07 reads 79 / HIGH / WELL_RECOVERED, but validSleep is false and sleepScoreFactorPercent is 0; it is a recoveryTime countdown (the limiting factor on 62 of 68 scored days) wearing a physiological label.
correctedFacts.soWhat: Any rocket feature rendering an HRV trend, sleep debt, or "HRV is down, back off" would be fabricated. What DOES exist and is dense: resting HR (143 days), body battery (153), all-day stress (161), respiration (147), recoveryTime (160) — all clearing a 14-of-21-day bar.

correctedFacts.topic: UNASKED — the export is 164 days, not "the full history"
correctedFacts.whatWeBelieved: This export lifts rocket from a 42-day API window to the athlete's full training history.
correctedFacts.whatTheDataSays: Account created 2026-03-28T18:46:24Z; device (fenix 8, unitId 3613943939, serial 8JZ058255) registered the same day; first activity 2026-03-28T20:25:27Z; first PR the same minute. Four independent files agree. Filename date ranges are export-partition labels, not data spans — UDSFile_2026-02-20_2026-05-31.json actually starts 2026-03-28, and every ..._20260706_20261014_... file ends 2026-09-07 with nothing future-dated. The only pre-2026 file, 2025-04-27_2025-08-05_..._sleepData.json, is an 18-byte stub.
correctedFacts.soWhat: rocket gains ~122 days over the API window, not years. A 42-day CTL seeded 2026-03-28 has ~3.9 time constants by today — just enough. But no CTL before roughly mid-May 2026 is defensible, and there is no deeper archive to fall back on.

synthesis.trainingLoadCurve:
METRIC: Garmin's per-activity `activityTrainingLoad` from summarizedActivities.json, summed per local day (startTimeLocal is epoch ms, already timezone-shifted, so decode UTC-naive), fed to standard TrainingPeaks EWMAs — CTL alpha = 1-exp(-1/42), ATL alpha = 1-exp(-1/7), TSB = CTL - ATL, seeded at 0 on 2026-03-28.

WHY THIS METRIC, NOT A DISTANCE PROXY: activityTrainingLoad is present on 56/56 activities (range 15.9-462.3, total 10,188.2), is EPOC-derived so it scales with both duration AND intensity, and — decisively — it is provably the input Garmin itself uses. dailyTrainingLoadAcute reproduces exactly as acute[t] = (7/55) × Σ(i=0..9) (10-i) × dailyLoad[t-i], max absolute error 0.52 load points across 132 days from 2026-04-25. A distance proxy would score the 2026-08-09 31.53 km at 6:34/km (load 339.5) as harder than the 2026-07-19 21.14 km at 5:02/km (load 431.5), which is backwards. aerobicTrainingEffect must NOT be used — it is censored at 5.0 on 10 of 56 sessions including the marathon. Load per km across the corpus is 17.32 (10,253 load / 592.01 km) and is used only for forward projection, never for backfill.

ONE ADJUSTMENT: the 2026-09-07 run is absent from summarizedActivities.json and carries no load figure. Estimated at 110 (36.26 min × ~3.0 load/min), bracketed by comparable HR-159 sessions — 2026-08-12 at 2.65/min, 2026-09-05 at 2.61/min on the low side, 2026-07-02 at 5.04/min on the high. Uncertainty ±20 load, which moves today's TSB by ±3.

TRAJECTORY (date | day load | CTL | ATL | TSB):

2026-08-02 | 491.5 | 72.3 | 116.9 | -44.6   <- ALL-TIME CTL PEAK 72.3

2026-09-05 | 144.3 | 56.2 |  40.8 | +15.4   <- treadmill 128.5 + hike 15.9

2026-09-07 | 110.0*| 56.2 |  45.3 | +10.9   <- the run the JSON does not have

(* estimated)

REFERENCE POINTS: CTL 7d ago 55.0, 14d ago 65.0, 21d ago 69.1, 28d ago 68.8, 42d ago 64.0. CTL is down 15.9% in 14 days and 24.2% from peak — a real but modest erosion, and the ATL collapse (116.9 → 39.2) is far steeper than the CTL loss, which is exactly the shape of a taper.

WITHOUT the orphan run the same day reads CTL 52.3 / ATL 26.5 / TSB +25.8, and race day CTL 47.6 / ATL 15.0 / TSB +32.6. The 10-point TSB difference is the cost of trusting the summary JSON alone.

GARMIN'S OWN VIEW, for cross-check only (do NOT seed CTL from it — different units, different estimators): dailyTrainingLoadAcute 228, dailyTrainingLoadChronic 253, ratio 0.9, acwrStatus OPTIMAL, chronic-minus-acute +25 on 2026-09-07. Garmin's acute is a triangular-weighted 10-day window, not a 7-day EWMA (it reaches exactly zero after 14 rest days, 2026-05-20 to 06-03; a true EWMA never does). Garmin's chronic decays daily like an EWMA but at a non-constant rate that no fixed alpha reproduces — observed zero-load decay ranges 0.55%/day (2026-07-06) to 7.95%/day (2026-09-03). Expect rocket's 42-day CTL to read materially higher than Garmin's chronic during sharp changes; that is a known, explainable divergence, not a bug. Exclude 2026-03-28..04-06 (chronic bootstrap, mirrors acute exactly) and 2026-06-03..06-18 (chronic frozen at 219 for 16 days, manufacturing the export's only VERY_HIGH readings) from any agreement metric.
synthesis.raceWeekRead:
VERDICT: the plan is too fast. Open at 4:55/km, not 4:45/km, and do not plan a 4:35/km move at all.

THE EVIDENCE, in order of weight:

1. His best-ever CONTINUOUS 21 km is 2026-07-19: 21.14 km at 5:02.4/km (1:46:33), avg HR 174, max 194, 0.6 min stopped, aerobicTrainingEffect 5.0 / VO2MAX, load 431.5. He ran that at CTL ~70 with TSB -44. Race-day CTL is 49.9 — 29% less chronic fitness. 4:45/km asks 17 s/km faster than that; 4:35/km asks 27 s/km faster.

2. The 1:44:44 "PR" (2026-07-26) is a training run with 16:02 of stopped time across 22 laps. Its 4:57.9/km is timer pace, not race pace, and the stops let HR recover — hence avg 165 against 174 on the unbroken 07-19 effort.

3. Garmin over-predicts this athlete by 8.8-13.0% on realised efforts. 5905 s × 1.118 (the cleanest calibration point — the continuous 07-19 half) = 6601 s = 1:50:01. That is the "run it like a July training run" floor.

4. Freshness pushes back, hard. TSB +27.7 on race day against -44 on 2026-07-19 is a 72-point swing. A race effort versus a solo training run is typically worth another 5-15 s/km, and Battersea is flat. That buys back roughly 4-7 minutes off the 1:50 floor.

5. Physiology is intact. VO2max 53.0, unchanged through the layoff. LT HR 177, LT pace 4:20.9/km (auto-detected 2026-08-08). Resting HR 57 smoothed / 50 raw on 2026-09-07 — the lowest raw since 2026-08-01 and 7-9 bpm under his summer baseline. Body battery never fell below 72 all day on 09-07 (joint 4th-highest trough of 151 measured days, median 42). Readiness 79/HIGH, recoveryTime 1 minute, acwrFactor 95% GOOD.

6. The countervailing fact rocket should surface rather than hide: 19.97 km of genuine running in 17 days, only 12.5 km of it outdoors on road, with a 10-day zero-running stretch. He is fresh but under-rehearsed at race pace. That is freshness bought with detraining.

TARGET: 4:55/km → 1:43:48. Run the first 5 km at 4:58 and let it settle. That is a decisive improvement on his best continuous half (1:46:33) and beats the stopped-clock PR outright.

FALLBACK: 5:05/km → 1:47:14. Take it if pace feels forced at 8 km or HR is 174+ at 10 km.

UPSIDE, conditional and unlikely: if he passes 10 km under 49:30 with HR under 165 — genuinely comfortable, not merely survivable — move to 4:45/km for the second half, landing ~1:41:30. Do not plan for it; earn it.

ON THE HR GATE: 170 is a sensible ceiling but the plan uses it backwards. 170 is 96% of his LT HR (177) and 85% of his real max (201, not the 196 in the profile). At 4:55/km expect 165-172 through 10 km, so "under 170" will be marginal and is not a signal to accelerate. Invert it — at 10 km: under 165 = press; 165-173 = hold; 174 or above = back off 5-10 s/km immediately, because 174 is the average he sustained on his hardest-ever half with 29% more chronic fitness underneath it.

ONE THING ROCKET MUST HANDLE BEFORE SATURDAY: the race itself breaches the single-session spike guardrail. Trailing-30-day longest run as of 2026-09-12 is 16.00 km (2026-08-22), giving a 110% cap of 17.60 km. The race is 21.0975 km = 131.9% of the window longest. Either exempt A-races or the app fires a false alarm on race morning. (Note the 31.53 km run of 2026-08-09 that would have covered it sits exactly on the window boundary today, 2026-09-08, and drops out tomorrow.)
synthesis.blockFeasibility:
NOT SUPPORTABLE. The 100 km peak is roughly double what the data justifies, and week 1 at 60 km already exceeds his best week ever. Four independent lines of evidence say no.

1. HIGHEST REAL WEEK ON RECORD: 57.12 km, week commencing 2026-05-04 (3 runs, load 774.4). Second highest 48.00 km (2026-04-20). Across 24 complete weeks he averaged 24.35 km/wk (584.36 km total). Week 1 of the plan exceeds his all-time maximum by 5%. Week 3 is 1.75× it.

2. RECENT BASE: the four complete weeks to 2026-08-31 are 27.16 / 34.77 / 0.00 / 14.83 km — mean 19.2 km/wk, 76.76 km total. Week 1 at 60 km is a 3.1× jump off that base. Even his strongest sustained block (the 8 weeks 2026-06-28 to 2026-08-22) averaged only 35.17 km/wk.

3. GARMIN'S OWN CEILING: RunningTolerance acuteTolerance is 40,627 impact units as of 2026-09-07, with current load 11,480 = 28% of it (phrase LOW_LOAD_7DAYS). At the measured corpus rate of 1,185 impact units per km (637,350 units / 537.67 km over 19 weeks) that is ~34.3 km/week. A 100 km week is 118,540 units = 2.92× the ceiling; 80 km is 2.33×; 60 km is 1.75×. All five planned weeks are ABOVE_TOLERANCE by Garmin's own rule from week one. Tolerance would need to grow +19,478/week for four consecutive weeks; the best single weekly rise ever observed is +7,096 and the mean during his strongest build was +1,282. Even extrapolating the best-ever rate lands at 69,011 units = 58 km-equivalent, 42% short of 100 km. The all-time maximum tolerance he has ever reached is 60,516 (early May) ≈ 51 km/week — and tolerance is currently FALLING (46,551 on 08-23 → 42,531 on 09-02 → 40,627 on 09-06).

4. THE PROJECTION BREAKS. Simulating the asked-for block at 17.32 load/km with a 20/15/20/15/30 weekly distribution: week 1 ends at ACWR 1.76, week 2 at 1.99, week 3 at 2.04 with TSB -122. Garmin has never rated this athlete above 1.8, and the only VERY_HIGH readings in the entire export (2026-06-14/15/16, ratios 2.3/2.0/1.7) are artefacts of a frozen chronic value, not real training. A sustained ACWR near 2.0 for three weeks is the textbook shape of a week-three breakdown.

THE NUMBER THE DATA SUPPORTS: peak 50 km, in week 3.

  wk1  2026-09-14   35 km   long run 21 km
  wk2  2026-09-21   42 km   long run 23 km
  wk3  2026-09-28   50 km   long run 25 km   <- PEAK
  wk4  2026-10-05   44 km   long run 27 km
  wk5  2026-10-12   34 km   long run 20 km
  wk6  2026-10-19   22 km   + marathon 2026-10-24

Projected: peak ACWR 1.58 (week 3), race-eve CTL 79.1 / ATL 71.4 / TSB +7.7. That race-eve CTL of 79 EXCEEDS his all-time peak of 72.3 — this is a better marathon platform than he has ever stood on, built without a single week above his personal record. Total build volume 227 km.

CEILING IF WEEKS 1-2 LAND CLEAN: 38/46/55/46/36 is defensible (peak ACWR 1.64, race-eve CTL 82.9). Decide at the end of week 2 on evidence — resting HR flat or trending down, no LOW readiness days, no ABOVE_TOLERANCE phrase. Do not decide it now.

THE LONG RUN IS THE REAL CONSTRAINT, NOT THE WEEKLY TOTAL. Saturday's 21.1 km resets the trailing-30-day window to 21.10 km through 2026-10-12, giving a 110% cap of 23.21 km. The tightest legal ladder from there is 21 → 23 → 25 → 27 → 20 km, putting a 27 km longest run three weeks before the marathon. His 3:53:05 in May came off a 30.11 km long run four weeks out. He arrives slightly under-prepared on distance, which is unavoidable in six weeks and is the price of the August gap. The marathon itself (42.2 km = 156% of a 27 km longest) breaches the guardrail no matter what — that needs a race exemption, not a plan change. Without Saturday's race resetting the window, the block would start against a 17.60 km cap and by 2026-09-28 the cap would fall to 11.00 km (or 8.24 km once the treadmill distance is corrected to 7.489 km), which makes any marathon build structurally illegal.

WHY 50 AND NOT 60: 60 km in week 3 pushes ACWR to ~1.7 and lands within 5% of his all-time max week off a 19 km/wk base. The athlete said he would rather be told now than break down in week three. 50 km is the number that survives that test.

backfillSpec.target: activities table, keyed on activityId (unique, no duplicates)
backfillSpec.rationale: The primary load source. distance/100000 = km, duration/60000 = timer minutes, elapsedDuration/60000 = elapsed, movingDuration/60000 = Garmin's own moving figure (a THIRD value, mean 255 s below timer, matching nothing in the FIT — store it but never use it as either elapsed or timer). Records are NOT chronologically sorted; sort by startTimeLocal before any windowing. startTimeLocal - startTimeGmt takes four values (0h, +1h, +2h, -7h) — the athlete recorded in at least three timezones.

backfillSpec.target: the per-session load input to rocket's existing CTL(42d)/ATL(7d)/TSB engine
backfillSpec.rationale: Proven to be Garmin's own input: acute[t] = (7/55)·Σ(10-i)·dailyLoad[t-i] reproduces dailyTrainingLoadAcute to within 0.52 points over 132 days. Sum per local day. Do NOT use aerobicTrainingEffect (censored at 5.0 on 10 of 56 sessions). Do NOT seed CTL/ATL from Garmin's chronic/acute — different units (EPOC load points, not TSS) and different estimators.

backfillSpec.target: activities table, as a distinct session with a synthetic id and a provenance flag
backfillSpec.rationale: 7.65 km / 36:16 / avg HR 159 — real training load that exists in no JSON. Without it today's TSB reads +25.8 instead of +15.6. Join FITs to activities on file_id.time_created vs startTimeGmt/1000 (tolerance 2 s; max observed offset 1.0 s across 56 pairs). NEVER join on filename — 12-digit upload ids, zero overlap with 11-digit activityIds.

backfillSpec.target: an ingest-time reconciliation gate; quarantine activityId 24251846565's distance
backfillSpec.rationale: Catches the 2026-09-05 treadmill corruption (10000.0 top-level vs 7488.69 in the split) with no FIT parsing required. Across all 56 activities this is the ONLY case where the two disagree by more than 5 m, so the check has a zero false-positive rate on this corpus. Flag ratio outside 1.00 ± 0.01. disagreementsWithGarmin: ACWR band. Garmin calls ratios up to 1.4 OPTIMAL (124 records span 0.8-1.4), wider than the 0.8-1.3 sweet spot usually cited. If rocket flags >1.3 as risky it will contradict the watch on the athlete's wrist on 23 days of this export. Pick the threshold deliberately and document it, or the app warns on days Garmin calls fine.

Chronic-load estimator. Garmin's dailyTrainingLoadChronic decays daily like an EWMA but at a NON-CONSTANT rate — observed zero-load decay ranges 0.55%/day (2026-07-06) to 7.95%/day (2026-09-03), so no fixed alpha reproduces it. Its effective memory is roughly 15-31 days against rocket's 42. During the current decline Garmin reads -63% from peak where rocket's CTL reads -24%. Expect and explain the gap; do not treat it as a bug in either direction.

Acute-load estimator. Garmin's acute is NOT an EWMA at all — it is a triangular-weighted 10-day window, acute[t] = (7/55)·Σ(10-i)·dailyLoad[t-i], with a hard cutoff at lag 10 (max error 0.52 points over 132 days). It reaches exactly zero after 14 consecutive rest days (2026-05-20 to 06-03); a true EWMA never does. rocket's 7-day EWMA has a longer tail to day 10 and a shorter one beyond, so the two will not agree even in steady state on a variable schedule.

Race prediction. Garmin says 1:38:25 for the half and 3:36:12 for the marathon. Against three realised efforts it runs 8.8-13.0% optimistic, including a 26:49 miss on the marathon it predicted the morning of. rocket should surface the calibrated figure (×1.118 ≈ 1:50:01 before adjusting for taper and race effect), with the raw prediction shown as the ceiling.

Marathon extrapolation. Garmin's own marathon prediction is 11 minutes SLOWER than a Riegel 1.06 extrapolation from its own half prediction on the same day (12,972 s actual vs 12,313 s from 5905 × 2^1.06). rocket must not derive one from the other and expect Garmin's number.

ACWR display fields. acwrPercent is a gauge position, not ACWR×100 (ratio 1.0 maps to 42), and it saturates at 100 for any ratio ≥ 2.0. Separately, TrainingReadinessDTO.acwrFactorPercent reads 95 on 2026-09-07 for the same ratio of 0.9 where MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad.acwrPercent reads 38 — two near-identically-named percent fields on unrelated scales. Use dailyAcuteChronicWorkloadRatio and replicate its FLOOR truncation to 1 dp (rounding disagrees with Garmin on 109 of 252 days).

Running tolerance vs the Nielsen spike rule. Garmin's tolerance is a per-WEEK impact-load ceiling; rocket's guardrail is a per-SESSION distance rule. They catch different failures and both should run. Garmin's is currently the more binding: all five weeks of the proposed block breach it from week one, and Garmin's own feedback phrase has already fired ABOVE_TOLERANCE on 2026-08-22 (ratio 1.09) and on the week of 2026-08-09 (1.226).
Hill Score. 38 and unchanged since 2026-08-22, because it only updates on uphill running. Battersea is flat. Do not read it as a fitness signal for either race.

Fitness age. currentBioAge (28.44 → 24.32) is a near-linear restatement of resting heart rate — RHR is the only continuously moving input, with BMI frozen at 27.046 and chronological age constant at 27. Feeding it alongside RHR double-counts the same signal.

Readiness. Garmin's readiness score is not a holistic recovery measure for this athlete — hrvFactorPercent and stressHistoryFactorPercent are 0 with feedback NONE on 267/267 records, and recoveryTime is the limiting factor on 62 of 68 scored days. It is a recovery-timer countdown. Ingest it labelled as such, or rocket implies a physiological signal that was never computed.

mined.schemaNotes:
ROOT: `json.load(f)` -> list[1] -> dict with single key `summarizedActivitiesExport` -> list[56] of activity dicts. Records are NOT sorted by time in the file; sort by `startTimeLocal` yourself.

=== UNIT SYSTEM (all verified two ways; see findings) ===
- distance: CENTIMETRES (float). km = distance/100000.
- duration / elapsedDuration / movingDuration: MILLISECONDS (float).
- avgSpeed / maxSpeed / avgGradeAdjustedSpeed / maxVerticalSpeed: cm/ms. m/s = value * 10. (The brief's claim "numerically equal to m/s" is WRONG — 0.3386 means 3.386 m/s, a factor of 10.)
- elevationGain / elevationLoss / minElevation / maxElevation: CENTIMETRES. metres = value/100.
- avgStrideLength: CENTIMETRES.
- calories / bmrCalories: KILOJOULES, not kcal. kcal = value/4.184.
- hrTimeInZone_0..6 and powerTimeInZone_0..5: MILLISECONDS.
- beginTimestamp / startTimeGmt / startTimeLocal: epoch MILLISECONDS. startTimeLocal is pre-shifted; decode with a UTC-naive conversion. Offsets present in this file: -7h, 0h, +1h, +2h (timeZoneId in {121,124,159}).
- avgHr/maxHr/minHr: bpm (float). avgPower/maxPower/normPower: watts.
- avgGroundContactTime: milliseconds. avgVerticalOscillation: cm. avgVerticalRatio: percent.
- waterEstimated: millilitres (~15.9 ml/min average).
- steps: count. avgRunCadence = avgDoubleCadence/2 (single-leg vs total steps/min; max observed disagreement 0.96, it is a truncation artefact). avgFractionalCadence / maxFractionalCadence: dimensionless 0-1 fractional part.

=== NESTED STRUCTURES ===
`splitSummaries`: list of dicts, one per split *type*. Keys: noOfSplits int, duration float SECONDS (not ms — differs from the top level), type int, maxDistance int m, maxDistanceWithPrecision float m, distance float METRES, averageSpeed float TRUE m/s (not cm/ms — differs from the top level), maxSpeed float m/s, avgStepFrequency float spm, avgStepLength float METRES, verticalRatio, verticalOscillation, avgGroundContactTime. Observed `type` codes: 3 = whole session, 17 = active/running portion, 18 = walk/recovery portion, 22 = pause/idle blocks. mined.rocketRelevance:
BACKFILL IT, with three carve-outs.

Backfill: all 56 records, keyed on activityId (unique, no dupes). Use `distance`/100000 for km, `movingDuration`/60000 for moving time, `duration`/60000 for elapsed-training time, and `activityTrainingLoad` as the per-session load input to the CTL(42d)/ATL(7d) EWMAs. activityTrainingLoad is present on 100% of records, is EPOC-derived, and scales correctly with both duration and intensity — it is the right TSS substitute here. Do NOT use aerobicTrainingEffect as the load quantity: it is capped at 5.0 and 10 of 56 sessions are at the cap. Keep aerobicTrainingEffect / anaerobicTrainingEffect / trainingEffectLabel as a per-session intensity classifier, and keep hrTimeInZone_0..6 (a complete ms partition of duration) as an independent TRIMP cross-check if you ever want to sanity-check Garmin's own number.

Carve-out 1 — treadmill_running SHOULD count toward training load. Same sportType (RUNNING), same device, same HR/TE/power/running-dynamics fields, same mechanical stress on the athlete. Excluding it would silently zero out a real 42.8-minute session on 2026-08-15 in the middle of a build week. BUT trust its TIME and LOAD, not its DISTANCE: the 2026-09-05 record's distance is an overridden 10.00 km against a raw 7.49 km. Recommend: include treadmill time and activityTrainingLoad in CTL/ATL unconditionally; include treadmill distance in weekly km with a provenance flag; EXCLUDE treadmill from the single-session spike guardrail, because the guardrail compares distances and treadmill distance is athlete-entered, not measured.

Carve-out 2 — hiking SHOULD NOT count. Three reasons, in order of strength. (a) The guardrail is a distance comparison and hiking distance is not commensurate with running distance: 12.0-12.4 min/km moving pace is walking, and letting a 6 km hike raise the 30-day longest-run ceiling would be a false negative in exactly the direction that hurts. (b) `duration` on hikes is 2.6-3.6x `movingDuration`, so any duration-based load term is inflated by standing around. (c) The load is immaterial anyway: both hikes together are 44.9 aTL out of 10188.2 total, 0.44%. Excluding them costs nothing and avoids two classes of error. If you want them represented at all, add their activityTrainingLoad to CTL/ATL only (44.9 total) and keep them out of weekly km and out of the guardrail entirely.

Carve-out 3 — the spike guardrail needs a race exemption and a stale-window rule before Saturday. As it stands the 2026-09-12 half (21.1 km) breaches its own 17.60 km cap, and the 2026-06-10/2026-06-14 historic "breaches" are artefacts of the 23-day layoff emptying the 30-day window rather than real spikes. Two concrete needs: exempt A-race sessions from the guardrail, and define behaviour when the trailing window contains fewer than N runs or the athlete is returning from a gap — otherwise the first run back always trips it.

CROSS-CHECK AGAINST: whatever rocket already holds from the ~42-day Garmin API window. The overlap is roughly 2026-07-28 to 2026-09-08, about 15 activities. Reconciling activityId, distance and activityTrainingLoad across that overlap will confirm the API and the export use the same units (they may not — the API typically returns metres and seconds where this export returns centimetres and milliseconds) before you trust the backfill of the 41 older records.

domains.title: Garmin's own acute training load and training history

mined.domain: Garmin's own computed acute/chronic training load and training-status history (MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad + TrainingHistory, both date windows)
mined.recordCounts:
MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad: 180 records (file 1) + 89 (file 2) = 269 raw, 268 distinct (calendarDate,timestamp) keys. TrainingHistory: identical counts, 180 + 89 = 269 raw / 268 distinct. The one duplicate is the window-boundary day 2026-07-06, timestamp 1783321671000, which appears in both files with a byte-identical payload (verified by object equality) — dedupe on (calendarDate,timestamp), do not sum.

Date coverage (both families identical): 2026-03-28 to 2026-09-07, 160 distinct calendar days out of a 164-day span. Four days are entirely absent: 2026-08-29, 08-30, 08-31, 09-01. Records are NOT one-per-day — 160 days carry 268 records because the watch writes multiple snapshots on days with activity (up to 4/day); 16 days contain more than one distinct trainingStatus within the same day. Take the record with the max timestamp per calendarDate to build a daily series.

Cross-check file: summarizedActivities holds 56 activities spanning 2026-03-28 to 2026-09-05, on 53 distinct days, all 56 carrying a non-null activityTrainingLoad.
mined.schemaNotes:
Both file families are a flat JSON array of objects. No nesting anywhere — zero sub-objects, zero arrays inside records. Field presence varies per record (optional keys are simply absent, never null).

=== MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad_*.json ===
- userProfilePK: int. Constant 144449296. Garmin user id.
- calendarDate: int, EPOCH MILLISECONDS. All 269 values satisfy v % 86400000 == 0, i.e. exact UTC midnight — decode with utcfromtimestamp(v/1000).date(). NOTE: this is a different encoding from the same-named field in TrainingHistory.
- deviceId: int. Constant 3613943939.
- timestamp: int, epoch milliseconds. Wall-clock moment the watch wrote the snapshot (e.g. 1774686290000 = 2026-03-28T08:24:50Z). Use it to pick the last record of a day.
- dailyTrainingLoadAcute: int. Unitless Garmin load points (EPOC-derived), scaled as a 7-day-equivalent. Observed range 0..1008.
- dailyTrainingLoadChronic: int. Same unit and same 7-day-equivalent scale. Observed range 113..677.
- dailyAcuteChronicWorkloadRatio: float, 1 decimal place. Present 252/269. Unitless.
- acwrPercent: int 0..100. Present 263/269. NOT a percentage of anything — a display-gauge position (see unitTraps).
- acwrStatus: string enum, present 269/269. Values: NONE, LOW, OPTIMAL, HIGH, VERY_HIGH.
- acwrStatusFeedback: string enum, present 269/269. Values: NONE, FEEDBACK_1..FEEDBACK_5. Fully determined by acwrStatus and ratio: LOW->FEEDBACK_1 (107/107), HIGH->FEEDBACK_4 (19/19), VERY_HIGH->FEEDBACK_5 (6/6), NONE->NONE (6/6), OPTIMAL splits FEEDBACK_2 (ratio 0.8-1.2, 108) / FEEDBACK_3 (ratio 1.3-1.4, 23). Carries no information beyond status+ratio.

=== TrainingHistory_*.json ===
- userProfilePK: int, same constant.
- calendarDate: STRING "YYYY-MM-DD" (e.g. "2026-03-28"). Different type from the acute-load file's epoch-ms int for the identically-named field.
- deviceId: int, same constant.
- timestamp: STRING "YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS.0" with a trailing ".0" and NO timezone suffix (e.g. "2026-03-28T08:24:50.0"). It is the same instant as the acute-load file's epoch-ms timestamp rendered as UTC — verified: joining A on utc(timestamp)[:19] to H on timestamp[:19] yields 268/268 matches with zero left-only and zero right-only keys. So despite the naming, this string is UTC, not local.
- trainingStatus: string enum, present 269/269. Values: NO_STATUS, MAINTAINING, RECOVERY, PEAKING, PRODUCTIVE, DETRAINING.
- fitnessLevelTrend: string enum, present 263/269 (absent on the first 6 records only). Values: INCREASING, NO_CHANGE, NO_RESULT.
- trainingStatus2FeedbackPhrase: string, present 269/269. A message key, always prefixed by the status: PRODUCTIVE_2/_3/_7/_9, RECOVERY_1/_2, MAINTAINING_2/_4, PEAKING_1, DETRAINING, NO_STATUS_1/_2.
- sport: string, present 239/269, only ever "RUNNING". Absent on days with no activity.
- subSport: string, present 239/269, only ever "GENERIC".

=== Join contract ===
The two families are the SAME event stream with disjoint payloads, written by the same device at the same instants. Join 1:1 on (calendarDate, timestamp) — 268 keys, perfect intersection, no orphans on either side. A parser can materialise one daily row: acute, chronic, ratio, acwrStatus, trainingStatus, fitnessLevelTrend.

No nested objects, no load-focus/anaerobic/aerobic breakdown, and no CTL/ATL/TSB-named fields exist in any of the four files.

findings.claim: Garmin DOES expose acute and chronic load figures, and they are directly analogous to ATL and CTL — but they are not EWMAs and not on a TSS scale. Field names are dailyTrainingLoadAcute (ATL analogue) and dailyTrainingLoadChronic (CTL analogue), both in MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad_*.json.
findings.value: Most recent values, 2026-09-07 (last record in the export, timestamp 2026-09-07T07:23:42Z): dailyTrainingLoadAcute = 228, dailyTrainingLoadChronic = 253, dailyAcuteChronicWorkloadRatio = 0.9, acwrPercent = 38, acwrStatus = OPTIMAL. Garmin's TSB analogue (chronic - acute) = +25.
findings.derivation: MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad_20260706_20261014_144449296.json, final record by max timestamp; calendarDate 1788307200000 -> 2026-09-07. Units are Garmin load points (EPOC-derived), NOT TSS — a rocket CTL of e.g. 55 TSS/day is not comparable in magnitude to a Garmin chronic of 253.

findings.claim: dailyTrainingLoadAcute has an EXACT closed form and it is a triangular-weighted 10-day window, not a 7-day EWMA. rocket's 7-day EWMA ATL will systematically disagree with the watch unless this is accounted for.
findings.value: acute[t] = (7/55) * sum_{i=0..9} (10-i) * dailyLoad[t-i]. Weight sum = 7, so a steady daily load L yields acute = 7L (hence 'seven-day-equivalent'). Weights: 1.2727, 1.1455, 1.0182, 0.8909, 0.7636, 0.6364, 0.5091, 0.3818, 0.2545, 0.1273; zero at lag >= 10.
findings.derivation: Least-squares fit of dailyTrainingLoadAcute against 10 lags of daily summed activityTrainingLoad (from summarizedActivities, startTimeLocal read as UTC) over the 132 days from 2026-04-25: R^2 = 1.0000, weights exactly linear with common difference 7/55 = 0.12727. Closed form then verified directly: max absolute error 0.52 load points across all 132 days, mean 0.23, and 132/132 within 1.0 — the residual is pure integer rounding.

findings.claim: dailyTrainingLoadChronic IS an exponentially-weighted moving average, but with a ~31-day time constant, not TrainingPeaks' 42-day CTL. It is also expressed on the same 7-day-equivalent scale as acute.
findings.value: chronic[t] ~= 0.968 * chronic[t-1] + 0.032 * 7 * dailyLoad[t]. alpha = 0.968 (approx exp(-1/31)); EWMA N = 1/(1-alpha) = 31.3 days; half-life 21.4 days. Mean absolute one-step error 7.1 load points on a base of ~450 (~1.5%).
findings.derivation: Alpha swept 0.9500-0.9899 in 1e-4 steps, minimising mean one-step-ahead absolute error over the 75 consecutive-day pairs from 2026-06-20 (chosen to exclude the frozen-chronic stretch and the device warm-up). Best alpha 0.9681, err 7.089. Alternatives rejected: uniform 28-day window mean abs err 22.1 (4.9% rel), triangular-28 47.5, uniform-42 79.9 — and no fixed window can reproduce the smooth decay Garmin shows on zero-load days (e.g. 2026-08-23..28 chronic 497->482->468->451->430->408 with zero load, while a 28-day sum stays flat at 484).

findings.claim: dailyAcuteChronicWorkloadRatio is FLOOR-truncated to one decimal, not rounded. Naively recomputing it as round(acute/chronic,1) disagrees with Garmin on 109 of 252 days.

The chronic EWMA fit (alpha 0.968) is derived from 75 consecutive-day pairs in one regime (2026-06-20 onward) and reproduces one-step-ahead moves to ~1.5%; it has NOT been validated across the layoff or the freeze periods, where Garmin clearly applies extra logic. surprises: The brief calls this export 'the full history' versus the ~42-day Garmin API window. It is 164 days, not years. On a like-for-like basis the EWMA loses badly: free-running alpha=0.9681 level simulation over the same window gives mean abs err 80.6 (max 179.9) versus uniform-28's 22.1. It does beat persistence (7.02 vs 21.96 one-step), so there is real signal — but 'chronic IS an EWMA with a 31-day time constant' is not supported. The chronic-load model comparison is metric-mismatched and its conclusion does not follow. The EWMA's 7.089 is a one-step-ahead error seeded with yesterday's TRUE chronic; the rejected window models' 22.1 / 47.5 / 79.9 are LEVEL errors (I reproduced all three exactly on that basis). Like-for-like, a free-running alpha=0.9681 level simulation scores 80.6 mean abs error (max 179.9) against uniform-28's 22.1, and the best level-fit alpha is 0.935 (N=15.4 days, not 31.3). Decisively, a fixed alpha implies a constant zero-load decay ratio; the observed ratio ranges 0.9205-1.0079 over the fit window and 0.7534-1.0222 over the whole clean series (0.55%/day on 2026-07-06 vs 7.95%/day on 2026-09-03). Keep the miner's counterexample — uniform-28 really does sit flat at 484.4 across 2026-08-23..08-28 while Garmin decays 497->408 — and conclude that NEITHER model fits: chronic decays daily like an EWMA but at a non-constant rate. domains.title: Running tolerance — Garmin's own injury-risk ceiling

mined.domain: Running tolerance (Garmin's injury-risk ceiling) — RunningTolerance + RunningToleranceHistory
mined.recordCounts: Point-in-time (RunningTolerance): 144 + 83 = 227 rows over 147 distinct calendarDates, 2026-04-11 -> 2026-09-07. History (RunningToleranceHistory): 143 + 83 = 226 rows over 147 distinct calendarDates, 2026-04-05 -> 2026-09-07, spanning weekIndex 1892..1914 (23 weeks). Rows outnumber dates because Garmin writes multiple intraday snapshots on days with a run (up to 3). The two date-range files overlap on 2026-07-05/06 and carry non-identical intraday rows for those dates — dedupe on (calendarDate, timestampGMT, acuteImpactLoad) and keep the last, not first. Three consecutive days are absent from BOTH variants: 2026-08-30, 2026-08-31, 2026-09-01 (all zero-running days mid-break). Single deviceId 3613943939 throughout; primaryTrainingDevice is true on every row, so no multi-watch reconciliation needed.
mined.schemaNotes:
Both variants are a flat JSON array of objects; no nesting, no nulls, no missing keys (every field present on 100% of rows).

RunningTolerance_*.json (point-in-time, 9 fields):
  userProfilePK   int    144449296
  deviceId        int    3613943939
  calendarDate    str    "YYYY-MM-DD" — the day the snapshot is FOR (local). NOT epoch ms; unlike summarizedActivities these are ISO strings.
  timestampGMT    str    "YYYY-MM-DD" — date-only, and it is the *previous* day on rows written before the day's run; on run days a second row appears with timestampGMT == calendarDate. Treat calendarDate as the key.
  acuteImpactLoad int    decaying trailing running-impact load, Garmin impact-load units (see unitTraps)
  acuteDistance   int    METRES, strict trailing-7-day sum of running distance
  acuteTolerance  int    the ceiling, same impact-load units as acuteImpactLoad
  runningToleranceFeedBackPhrase str  enum, 8 values observed:
        MEDIUM_LOAD (56), LOW_LOAD_1DAYS (46), LOW_LOAD_7DAYS (38),
        HIGH_LOAD_WAS_ABOVE_TOLERANCE (27), ABOVE_TOLERANCE_ONE_HARD_RUN (24),
        LOW_LOAD_14DAYS (18), ABOVE_TOLERANCE (16), HIGH_LOAD (2)
  primaryTrainingDevice bool

RunningToleranceHistory_*.json (weekly accumulator, 9 fields):
  userProfilePK, deviceId, calendarDate, timestampGMT, primaryTrainingDevice — identical semantics
  totalImpactLoad int    week-to-date RAW (undecayed) sum of impact load, resets each week
  totalDistance   float  METRES, week-to-date raw sum (float, but always integral)
  tolerance       int    same value as acuteTolerance on the same calendarDate — one shared series
  weekIndex       int    week counter; weeks run SUNDAY 00:00 -> SATURDAY. weekIndex 1892 == week of 2026-03-29..2026-04-04. It is NOT weeks-since-1970 (1892*7 days from 1970-01-01 lands on 2006-04-06); treat it as an opaque monotonic key and derive dates from calendarDate.

How the two differ, precisely: the point-in-time file is a DECAYED trailing window (impact load bleeds off over ~10 days) compared against the ceiling; the history file is a RAW Sunday-reset weekly accumulator compared against the same ceiling. Same `tolerance` number, two different numerators. The history file is what the watch's weekly bar chart draws; the point-in-time file is the live "running tolerance" gauge. Neither carries a distance-denominated ceiling.

findings.claim: acuteDistance and totalDistance are in METRES (7-day rolling / week-to-date sums of running distance), not centimetres like summarizedActivities.distance
findings.value: 1 unit = 1 m
findings.derivation: Cross-checked against summarizedActivities.json (distance/100000 = km). 2026-08-22: acuteDistance=46156 vs sum of runs 2026-08-16..08-22 = 46.158 km = 46158 m (Δ 2 m). 2026-04-12: 45760 vs 45.761 km. 2026-09-05: 14834 vs 14.835 km. 2026-08-20: 35908 vs 35.911 km. Four independent dates, all within 3 m. Second derivation: RunningToleranceHistory weekIndex 1913 totalDistance=14834.0 equals the two runs in the Sun 08-30..Sat 09-05 week (4.835 + 10.000 km = 14.835 km).

findings.claim: Impact load (acuteImpactLoad / totalImpactLoad / tolerance) is a dimensionless Garmin unit, NOT distance and NOT Training-Load points; empirically ~1185 units per outdoor kilometre for this athlete
findings.value: 1185 impact-load units per km (aggregate); per-week range 1070–1360; treadmill runs ~750–1000
findings.derivation: RunningToleranceHistory, last row of each weekIndex: sum(totalImpactLoad)=637350 over sum(totalDistance)=537.67 km -> 1185.4 units/km. Per-week min 949 (weekIndex 1913, treadmill-dominated) / max 1360 (1905); excluding 1913 the aggregate is 1192.1. Mean of 19 weekly ratios 1191.9, median 1202.7. Independent check on a single-run week: weekIndex 1897 = one activity (Leeds marathon 2026-05-10, 42.667 km from summarizedActivities) with totalImpactLoad 45860 -> 1075 units/km. Scale is clearly distinct from Garmin Training Load (MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad shows dailyTrainingLoadAcute=228 for the same period — two orders of magnitude apart).

findings.claim: MOST RECENT TOLERANCE: 40,627 impact-load units, computed 2026-09-06 (timestampGMT) and carried on calendarDate 2026-09-07 — the last row in the export
findings.value: tolerance = 40627 (≈ 34.3 km/week equivalent)
findings.derivation: Final row of RunningTolerance_20260706_20261014_*.json: {calendarDate 2026-09-07, timestampGMT 2026-09-06, acuteImpactLoad 11480, acuteDistance 14834, acuteTolerance 40627, LOW_LOAD_7DAYS}. Identical `tolerance` 40627 in the final RunningToleranceHistory row (weekIndex 1914). km-equivalent = 40627 / 1185.4 = 34.3 km/week (range 29.9 km at 1360 units/km to 38.0 km at 1070).

findings.claim: Current acute state is deeply detrained: impact load is at 28% of tolerance, the lowest sustained reading since the May layoff, 5 days before the half marathon
findings.value: acuteImpactLoad 11480 / tolerance 40627 = 0.283; trailing-7-day distance 14.83 km
findings.derivation: RunningTolerance final row. Corroborated by summarizedActivities: an 11-day zero-running gap 2026-08-23 -> 2026-09-01 after the 16.0 km run of 2026-08-22, then only 4.835 km (09-02) and 10.0 km treadmill (09-05). RunningToleranceHistory weekIndex 1914 (Sun 09-06 onward) totalImpactLoad = 0, totalDistance = 0.0.

findings.claim: Garmin DOES publish a ceiling, but only in impact-load units — there is no km-denominated recommended maximum anywhere in the export
findings.value: acuteTolerance / tolerance is the ceiling; grep for 'tolerance' across the entire unpacked export matches ONLY these four files
findings.derivation: `grep -ril tolerance` over /Users/luisdeburnay/garmin-export/2026-09-08/raw returns exactly the four RunningTolerance* files. The km ceiling below is MY conversion via the measured 1185 units/km, not a number Garmin states.

findings.claim: Tolerance peak-to-date and its full range across the export
findings.derivation: min/max over acuteTolerance across both point-in-time files (227 rows). The 60,516 peak follows the 2026-04-26 week (41.71 km) and the run-up to the 2026-05-10 marathon; it collapsed -7,688 on 05-10 and -9,145 on 05-24 during the post-marathon layoff.

findings.claim: THE DECISIVE COMPARISON — a 100 km peak week is ~2.9x Garmin's current ceiling and ~2.0x the highest ceiling this athlete has EVER recorded
findings.value: 100 km = 118,540 impact-load units vs tolerance 40,627 -> 2.92x. Even at the most favourable observed load/km (1070, treadmill-heavy) it is 2.63x. Against the all-time max tolerance of 60,516 it is still 1.96x.
findings.derivation: 100 km x 1185.4 units/km = 118,540. 118,540 / 40,627 = 2.918. Sensitivity: at 1070 units/km -> 107,000 / 40,627 = 2.63x; at 1360 -> 136,000 / 40,627 = 3.35x. Every week of the block breaches: 60 km = 71,124 units = 1.75x tolerance; 80 km = 94,832 = 2.33x. Garmin flags ABOVE_TOLERANCE at ratio > 1.0, so all five weeks of the 60/80/100/80/60 block are above-tolerance by Garmin's own rule, from week one.

findings.claim: Tolerance cannot grow fast enough to catch up: reaching 118,540 by the peak week would need ~+19,700/week, versus a best-ever observed rise of +7,096 and a build-block average of +1,282
findings.value: Required +19,693/week for 4 consecutive weekly updates. Observed weekly rises: 7096, 4692, 3790, 2695, 2547, 2095, 1904, 1881, 1052, 1005, 813, 569, 126, 2 (n=18 rises total). Mean rise during the strongest observed build (2026-06-27 -> 2026-08-23, 9 rises) = +1,282/week.
findings.derivation: Gap = 118,540 - 40,627 = 77,913 over 4 weekly updates (block starts 2026-09-14; peak is week 3, so tolerance updates on 09-20, 09-27, 10-04 plus the 09-13 update) = 19,478..19,693/week. Deltas computed by differencing the daily acuteTolerance series; all rises land on Sunday except four small intra-week nudges. Extrapolating even the best-ever +7,096/week from 40,627 gives 40,627 + 4x7,096 = 69,011 = 58.2 km-equivalent at the peak week — still 42% short of 100 km.

findings.claim: Garmin has never once seen this athlete complete a week above 47.3 km, and every week above ~46 km was already scored ABOVE_TOLERANCE
findings.value: Highest weekly volume in the export: 47.30 km (Sun 2026-08-09 week, weekIndex 1910, totalImpactLoad 50,630 vs tolerance 41,309 = 1.226x). Second: 46.16 km (weekIndex 1911, 52,920 vs 43,856 = 1.207x, phrase ABOVE_TOLERANCE on 2026-08-22).
findings.derivation: RunningToleranceHistory last-row-per-weekIndex, cross-checked against Sunday-start weekly sums of summarizedActivities running distance (identical to the metre). The planned 100 km peak is 2.11x the athlete's best week in the 23 weeks of data, and 2.35x his average across the 8-week 2026-06-28..2026-08-22 build (mean 38.2 km/wk).

findings.claim: No ACWR field exists in the RunningTolerance files; the ratio analogue is acuteImpactLoad / acuteTolerance and the overreaching flag is runningToleranceFeedBackPhrase
findings.value: Ratio range observed 0.00 – 1.58 (max 1.58 on 2026-08-09, acuteImpactLoad 65,075 vs tolerance 41,309, phrase ABOVE_TOLERANCE_ONE_HARD_RUN). 40 of 147 days (27%) sat above 1.0.
findings.derivation: Computed per calendarDate from the point-in-time file. Phrase thresholds inferred from the data: ratio >1.0 -> ABOVE_TOLERANCE or ABOVE_TOLERANCE_ONE_HARD_RUN (the latter when a single run dominates the window); ~0.85–1.0 after a breach -> HIGH_LOAD_WAS_ABOVE_TOLERANCE; ~0.5–0.85 -> MEDIUM_LOAD; <0.5 -> LOW_LOAD_{1,7,14}DAYS where the suffix is days since a qualifying run. A true acute:chronic ratio (acwrPercent, acwrStatus, dailyAcuteChronicWorkloadRatio) lives in MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad_*.json, a different metric on a different scale — do not conflate.

findings.claim: Impact load has a ~10-day memory, longer than the strict 7-day acuteDistance window — the two fields are NOT windows of the same length
findings.value: On 2026-05-17 acuteDistance = 0 (no run in trailing 7 days) while acuteImpactLoad = 24,530 (53% of the 2026-05-10 marathon's 45,860). It reached 0 only on 2026-05-20, 10 days post-run.
findings.derivation: Point-in-time file, 2026-05-17..2026-05-20 rows: acuteImpactLoad 24530, 18670, 9931, 0 with acuteDistance 0 throughout. Single-run decay isolated after 2026-09-02 (one 4.835 km run, raw load 6,590): 6593, 6286, 5952, 5586 on days 0..3 = retained fractions 1.000, 0.953, 0.903, 0.847 — an accelerating taper, not a flat 1/7 window and not a constant-rate exponential.

findings.claim: Tolerance updates weekly on Sunday and decays daily during inactivity; it is a slow adaptive chronic measure, roughly the trailing 4-week mean weekly impact load
findings.value: Best fit seen: tolerance on 2026-08-23 = 46,551 vs mean weekly totalImpactLoad of weekIndex 1908–1911 (38030, 45140, 50630, 52920) = 46,680 — 0.3% apart. Fit is looser earlier (2026-08-02: 39,428 vs 4-week mean 35,152, 12% high).
findings.derivation: 14 of 18 rises land on Sunday; falls of -350 to -460/day occur on consecutive inactive days (e.g. 2026-05-31..06-05: -512, -424, -411, -460, -395, -382), plus step falls at week boundaries after zero weeks (-9145 on 05-24, -6009 on 05-30, -4020 on 09-02, -1904 on 09-06). Treat the 4-week-mean fit as suggestive only, not a reproduced formula.

unitTraps: acuteDistance / totalDistance are METRES here, while summarizedActivities.distance is CENTIMETRES. Same concept, 100x apart, in the same export. A parser that reuses the summarizedActivities scaling will read 46156 m as 461.56 m and silently zero out the volume signal.
totalDistance is a float in the history file but an int (acuteDistance) in the point-in-time file. Always integral in practice; cast, do not assume.
calendarDate and timestampGMT are ISO date STRINGS ('2026-09-07'), not epoch milliseconds — the opposite of every timestamp field in summarizedActivities. No time component at all.

timestampGMT is usually calendarDate minus one day. Do not key on it. On days with a run there are 2–3 rows sharing a calendarDate; take the LAST by (timestampGMT, acuteImpactLoad) or you will read a stale pre-run snapshot.

acuteImpactLoad (decayed, ~10-day memory) and totalImpactLoad (raw, Sunday-reset week-to-date) are DIFFERENT numerators compared against the SAME tolerance. Mixing them understates a breach by ~10–15% (e.g. 2026-08-22: acute 47,732 vs raw week 52,920).
Impact load is not Garmin Training Load. Impact load runs 5,000–65,000; dailyTrainingLoadAcute in MetricsAcuteTrainingLoad runs ~200–300. Never add or compare them.

Treadmill runs generate ~20–35% less impact load per km (weekIndex 1913: 949 units/km with a 10 km treadmill run in a 14.8 km week, vs 1185 aggregate). Any km<->load conversion is biased by surface mix.
weekIndex is opaque. 1892*7 days from 1970-01-01 gives 2006-04-06, not 2026 — do not decode it arithmetically. Weeks are Sunday-start, Saturday-end; derive from calendarDate.
